title: Study Abroad Report: Children's Hospital of Philadelphia
paragraphs: I had the opportunity to do my clinical clerkship at CHOP, the children's hospital affiliated with Penn. I was attached to pediatric endocrinology, pediatric gastroenterology and pediatric pulmonology, and I was able to experience in a balanced way the three major parts of clinical work: pre-visit history taking in the outpatient clinic, caring for inpatients on the ward, and consultations. My experience in pediatric endocrinology, where I was assigned in the first month, is the most memorable, so I would like to talk about my study abroad experience starting with how the clerkship went there. In the first month every day was a series of tense moments, and everything I saw was fresh and stimulating. At first my English did not get across as I wanted and I felt frustrated, but in the end I was supported by the happy doctors and had an enjoyable month.

When I was in charge of inpatients, I would visit the ward early every morning and check the data on the PC and in the nursing records. I felt sorry for waking the parents, and I would quietly auscultate the children who were still sleeping soundly. Many of the parents were generous, and when I said I had come from Japan, they invariably cooperated gladly, which made me proud of my country. I also learned a great deal of the basics of endocrinology, such as adjusting insulin doses and the differential diagnosis of hypoglycemia. My team, including the boss, was made up entirely of women, so the morning rounds were fun and full of laughter. Nibbling on bagels or doughnuts that somebody had brought in, everyone made a fuss about whether the blood glucose had been several hundred or had improved. But when a question arose about the treatment plan, a serious discussion would suddenly begin. Questions that could not be resolved naturally led to "Then give us a lecture at tomorrow's round," and whoever got the assignment would look things up on PubMed and so on and give an easygoing lecture. In this way, without regard to rank, we exchanged up-to-date knowledge frankly within the team. However, at my tense first round, I spoke as if I were in a Japanese clinical clerkship, saying "So an increase in insulin is necessary," and everyone burst out laughing, saying "Thank you for the simple plan, Satoshi (laughs)." Here even students are asked for the dose of medication down to the mg. In my Polyclinic 1 clerkship I had only ever seen patients from behind a wall of people, so I was really at a loss. I read treatment manuals rather than textbooks, and I caught busy residents and asked them to teach me. When I finished presenting, in halting English, everything from the differential diagnosis to the plan, and someone said something like "Good work!", I was truly relieved. At first the residents were busy and did not pay attention to me. But when I kept at it every day, they began to let me examine their patients in the patient rooms when they had time and to give me lectures. This was very instructive, and talking about all sorts of things with the young residents was a very enjoyable time. The photo is a snapshot taken with the members at that time.

Every day was very academic, and after seeing an interesting disease I was immediately introduced to a paper. Sometimes the attending was the author of that paper. The next day I would be asked, "Did you read that paper?", so I worked hard to read it every night. Examining a child together with an authority in the field, reading papers and discussing them was an exciting experience. The unremarkable doctor sitting right next to you may turn out to be an authority whose papers fill the list when you search PubMed, so you cannot let your guard down. Whatever basic question a student, let alone a resident, asked was fine, and sometimes a casual question started a heated discussion among the doctors. I thought how much more interesting it was compared with the clinical clerkships in Japan. The children's hospital is highly specialized and subdivided, and extremely rare diseases gather there. I think it was a precious experience to see almost every day diseases that an average doctor would not see twice in a lifetime. I was also taken aback that many diseases that are uncommon in Japan or that I had only seen in textbooks came to the hospital, such as IBD in gastroenterology and CF in pulmonology, not to mention the enzyme and hormone disorders of endocrinology. I felt differences between their practice and ours in everyday care such as the management of DM and hypoglycemia and dietary guidance. In gastroenterology, I was also surprised that they did not understand glycyrrhizin.

When I belonged to the consult team in pulmonology, I spent most of my time in the pediatric ICU and saw many interesting cases. I learned that respiratory failure occurs from a wide variety of causes, not only lung disease but also neuromuscular diseases and rare hereditary diseases. For consults, we would go to the wards of other departments, decipher the past charts (the handwritten charts were almost code, and even the Americans had given up on them), and make a differential diagnosis and a plan. There were many times when we nearly ran out of time because of the sheer amount of history and the coded charts, but I was happy when they said "excellent!" and adopted my differential diagnosis as it was.

By the way, the biggest shock after coming to the United States was, in fact, that the doctors go home on time. Even the residents become restless as closing time approaches and suddenly leave. At first I interpreted it as "They must be doing experiments after this," but I was surprised to find that they really seem to go home (many senior physicians go back to their own labs even when off duty). When I stayed late for a journal club or a mini lecture (so typically Japanese), I was told, "Go home early and enjoy the spring sunshine." The work schedule is clear, and once the work is done they hand over and go home even at 4 o'clock. The person who takes over does a hard night shift, and after handing over the next morning, can go straight home. I suspect it ultimately comes down to the medical insurance system, but I am envious... I would also like to add that I played hard on weekends. Philly has an outstanding location, close to DC and NY, and the East Coast is an hour away by car (I rented a Harley and went touring). I strongly hope that the juniors who visit will enjoy their weekends. Philly is also an attractive city, and there were various pleasures such as first-class paintings, symphonies and jazz. The food was so varied, Chinese, Indian, African and Vietnamese, that you could almost go around the world (Japanese food, though...). I spent fulfilling weekends going out drinking with local medical students and enjoying the arts. I especially recommend the Barnes Collection, a private museum. It has a wonderful collection of Post-Impressionist works.

I was supported by a great many people. Dr. 伊藤 and Dr. 小林 of the International Exchange Office, Ms. 鈴木, Ms. 西尾, Dean 浜口, Dr. 西崎 of CHOP, Ms. Varelie of U-PENN and the doctors, the medical students, and K, who studied with me for three months. I have never spent three months so intense.
